articles.title: South Korea plans to relocate airbase for chip factories — The Japan Times - UA.NEWS
articles.summary: South Korea plans to relocate airbase for chip factories — The Japan Times  UA.NEWS
articles.full_text:
South Korea plans to relocate a military airfield in Gwangju, where it intends to develop a major semiconductor cluster. The freed-up area of 8.2 square kilometers is to become the central element of 800 trillion won in investment in four chip manufacturing plants by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, The Japan Times reports.
The project is part of President Lee Jae Myung's large-scale program, which provides for investments of 1,350 trillion won, or about $1 trillion, in semiconductors, physical artificial intelligence and data centers. The authorities aim to turn the southwestern Honam region into a technology hub. Last year, its economy contracted by 0.9%, while the country's economy grew by 1.1%.
Relocation of the airfield
The military facility in Gwangju is located about 266 kilometers from Seoul. Part of the territory is reserved for use by the U.S. military in the event of an emergency, so the relocation requires coordination with the United States. About 28,000 U.S. military personnel are stationed in South Korea, and Seoul has not said whether Washington has approved the relocation of the relevant facilities.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Previously, the government planned to relocate or temporarily disperse military facilities by mid-2028. The president instructed officials to consider the possibility of accelerating this process. Under the government's plan, the first of the four factories is to begin mass production by 2030.
U.S. pressure and infrastructure challenges
The plan could become another source of tension in relations with Washington. U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told Bloomberg Television that South Korea's expansion of its artificial intelligence sector should take place more in the United States and warned of the possibility of new tariffs.
After construction, the factories will need about 650,000 tonnes of water per day. The government expects to use water from nearby reservoirs and treated wastewater, although the region recently experienced a severe drought. The cluster is also expected to require new power transmission lines and about 23,000 workers. South Jeolla Province produces about twice as much electricity as it consumes, but the construction of new energy infrastructure has already sparked protests in rural communities.

Expert: "U.S. Stance on Taiwan Has Not Changed"
It has been argued that The Trump Administration should make active use of trilateral cooperation with South Korea and Japan to counter the threat of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan.
Alexander Gray, former White House National Security Council (NSC) chief of staff and deputy assistant to the president, said at a seminar hosted by the Stimson Center think tank in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 19 (local time) that the United States "should find ways to use trilateral cooperation with Japan and South Korea to defend Taiwan." Gray served in the first Trump Administration.
He cited China's economic retaliation against South Korea over its deployment of the THAAD missile defense system as an example of why cooperation among South Korea, the United States and Japan is necessary.
Gray said, "Imagine if such a framework had existed in 2017 or 2018. If Japan had joined the United States in helping ease some of South Korea's economic burden when China retaliated against major South Korean companies, including Lotte, over the THAAD deployment, it would have sent a very strong signal to China."
He stressed that "it is very important to extend regional cooperation frameworks, which exist mainly in the defense sector, to the economy and supply chains as well."
Gray also proposed using the Quad, a security partnership among the United States, Japan, Australia and India, to jointly respond to China's economic pressure on Taiwan.
Addressing controversy over the second Trump Administration's commitment to defending Taiwan, he said there had been no fundamental change in longstanding U.S. policy toward Taiwan. He added that the Trump Administration had not only maintained the United States' longstanding policy of defending Taiwan but had also strengthened it.
"President Trump has viewed Taiwan as the 'unsinkable aircraft carrier' of the Indo-Pacific," Gray said. "The way the United States views its relationship with Taiwan and formulates policy is fundamentally rooted in the same principles as U.S. policy toward Taiwan dating back to the Truman and Eisenhower administrations."
Gray also rejected suggestions that the United States' recent delay in a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan, worth about 20 trillion won, signaled a weakening commitment to Taiwan's defense, saying, "I absolutely disagree."
Michael Cunningham, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center, offered a different analysis, saying the Trump Administration was adjusting the timing of arms sales to Taiwan in consideration of its diplomatic relations with China.
"Successive U.S. presidents have adjusted the timing of arms sales to Taiwan to align with diplomatic schedules involving China," Cunningham said. "The sale will take place at the earliest toward the end of this year or early next year."

articles.title: South Korea Backs Chip Suppliers with $1.5B Guarantee, Shared Production Lab - Tech Times
articles.summary: South Korea Backs Chip Suppliers with $1.5B Guarantee, Shared Production Lab  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
South Korea and SK Hynix signed a ₩2 trillion guarantee agreement (approximately $1.5 billion) for domestic semiconductor materials, components, and equipment suppliers on Monday, deploying a government credit-leverage mechanism that the companies feeding the world's AI memory supply chain have struggled to access from ordinary banks.
The signing of the Export Supply Chain Strengthening Guarantee took place at SK Hynix's Yongin Cluster exhibition center in Gyeonggi Province, with CEO Kwak Noh-jung, Trade, Industry and Energy Minister Kim Jeong-kwan, representatives from the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation (K-SURE) and the four largest commercial banks — KB Kookmin, Shinhan, Woori, and Hana — and a cohort of materials, components, and equipment (MCE) supplier companies in attendance. First guarantee certificates were presented to qualifying suppliers at the ceremony.
The Ministry of Industry called the agreement the largest trade-finance deal of its kind involving a single company, and Minister Kim stated there was a need to accelerate the expansion of the semiconductor industry's domestic production capacity while stressing that construction safety must remain a priority.
Why Korean Chip Suppliers Cannot Get Ordinary Bank Financing
The guarantee program exists because South Korea's chip supply ecosystem faces a problem that no amount of fab expansion by Samsung or SK Hynix automatically solves: the hundreds of small to mid-sized companies that supply specialty gases, photoresists, CMP polishing compounds, deposition equipment, and inspection tools operate on thin balance sheets and limited access to credit. When SK Hynix's own expansion schedule accelerates — as it has throughout 2025 and 2026 — those supplier order books can swell faster than their working capital. South Korea's broader policy response to this fragility has included a ₩5 trillion national semiconductor investment fund announced in August.
But the deeper problem is not credit risk — it is information. A small Korean materials company that develops a new photoresist formulation suited for SK Hynix's next-generation HBM production cannot simply bring it to a bank and ask for a development loan. The bank cannot evaluate whether the material will pass SK Hynix's internal qualification standards, because qualification requires time on an actual running production line, in an environment that mirrors mass-production conditions. Without that qualification data, no lender can accurately price the credit risk, so lenders over-discount it — or decline entirely. The company cannot commercialize the material, which means it cannot generate the revenue needed to attract financing, which means it never gets on the fab line to generate the qualification data. This chicken-and-egg bottleneck is the structural problem Monday's two-part program is designed to fix.
How the 20x Leverage Mechanism Works
The financial structure addresses the risk-pricing half of the problem through leverage, not subsidy. SK Hynix and the four commercial banks together contribute a combined ₩100 billion (approximately $67 million) in capital to the program. The Korea Trade Insurance Corporation — South Korea's export credit agency — amplifies that contribution at 20-to-1, providing guarantees covering up to ₩2 trillion in supplier loans. The resulting terms significantly improve on standard K-SURE program limits across every dimension.
Under the enhanced terms, qualifying MCE suppliers receive expanded loan limits (raised 50% above what other industries receive under standard K-SURE programs), a guarantee ratio raised from 90% to 100% of the loan amount, an extended term of three years rather than the standard one, and interest rate cuts of up to 2.5 percentage points. The guarantee fee — typically borne by the borrower — is reduced by 25 to 35 percent by K-SURE, with the participating banks covering the residual for the full three years.
The mechanism is a formal instance of what K-SURE calls its SMILE program — Supply-chain Miracle by Leverage. The same structure, at a smaller scale, backed ₩630 billion in guarantees for Hyundai Motor Group's automotive suppliers in August 2025 after US tariffs disrupted that supply chain; extending it to semiconductors, and nearly tripling the scale, signals that Seoul has elevated chip supply-chain fragility to a strategic priority equivalent to automotive disruption. The government has stated it plans to extend the program to defense, nuclear energy, and biotechnology sectors, targeting a combined ₩10 trillion in guarantees by year-end.
Trinity Fab: Solving the Lab Access Problem
The guarantee mechanism handles credit risk transfer. The information asymmetry problem — the missing fab-validation data — is addressed by a separate facility announced alongside the guarantee program.
The Trinity Fab is a process-demonstration facility of approximately 3,300 square meters (roughly 35,500 square feet) being built inside the Y1 fab building at the Yongin Semiconductor Cluster. Backed by a ₩870 billion (approximately $580 million) joint investment from the central government, Gyeonggi Province, and SK Hynix, Trinity Fab is designed to give MCE suppliers access to a real semiconductor manufacturing environment — with the same process conditions as a mass-production line — where newly developed materials and equipment can be characterized and qualified without consuming commercial fab capacity.
SK Hynix has framed the facility explicitly as infrastructure for technological independence. Ceremony participants on Monday toured both the Trinity Fab site and the adjacent construction of the Y1 fab itself, which is scheduled to begin initial cleanroom operations in February 2027 — pulled forward from an earlier May 2027 target — and is intended to produce sixth-generation 10-nanometer-class (1c) DRAM and support HBM4E, the company's next-generation high-bandwidth memory chip for AI accelerator customers.
Trinity Fab is targeted to open in 2027. When it does, a Korean specialty gas or photoresist maker will be able to characterize its new formulation under production conditions, generate the qualification data that SK Hynix's engineers need to approve it for use, and return to a lender with that data as evidence of commercial viability — closing the information loop that the guarantee program alone cannot close.
"To secure the global competitiveness of South Korea's semiconductor industry at the national level and further strengthen the status of K-semiconductors, building a solid materials, parts and equipment ecosystem is essential," CEO Kwak said at the signing. "Based on support from this export supply chain fund and the creation of a one-stop technology verification environment through the Trinity Fab, we will join forces with our partners to further solidify technology leadership in the global semiconductor market."
What It Takes to Build One HBM Stack
Understanding why the MCE supplier ecosystem matters requires understanding what goes into a High Bandwidth Memory chip — the product at the center of South Korea's AI hardware dominance.
HBM is a three-dimensional memory architecture in which multiple thin DRAM silicon dies are stacked vertically, connected through thousands of microscopic Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) that run through the stacked layers like vertical wire bundles. The resulting stack is then placed on a silicon interposer adjacent to the host processor — typically an Nvidia GPU or a hyperscaler's AI accelerator — enabling data bandwidth that conventional memory could never achieve through a flat 2D layout. HBM3E, the current production standard, delivers approximately 1,229 gigabytes per second of bandwidth per stack; an eight-stack configuration yields roughly 9.8 terabytes per second.
SK Hynix pioneered HBM alongside AMD and now holds an estimated 53 to 58 percent HBM share globally. That dominance is built on successive generations of process refinement — and each new generation requires a fresh cycle of materials and equipment qualification. The CMP polishing compounds used to flatten each layer must be re-validated. The etch gases used to drill the TSV holes must perform consistently at new geometries. The photoresists that define circuit patterns must meet tighter specifications. Every one of those cycles requires fab time that MCE suppliers cannot otherwise access.
SK Hynix holds approximately 70% of Nvidia's HBM4 supply allocation for the Vera Rubin platform in 2026, according to analyst estimates, and generated first-half 2026 revenue of approximately $86.6 billion. The MCE suppliers that the guarantee program is designed to protect are the upstream companies that make the materials enabling that scale.
Why This Problem Is Harder for Korea Than for China
The information asymmetry and financing gap that South Korea is addressing through market mechanisms — credit leverage, shared validation infrastructure — is a structural problem that China's semiconductor industry does not face in the same way. Chinese chipmakers such as YMTC and CXMT operate within a state-ownership system that allows them to mandate adoption of domestic materials and equipment, providing domestically developed products with access to production environments as a matter of policy rather than commercial negotiation. Chinese MCE developers do not need to generate qualification data to attract financing, because the state can direct adoption before qualification is complete.
South Korea cannot use administrative mandates. SK Hynix is a publicly listed company. Its procurement decisions are commercially driven and subject to the same competitive logic that makes Korean chips attractive to Nvidia: they have to be the best available at acceptable cost. articles.title: South Korean Chipmakers Set for Strong 2027 on Memory Supply Crunch - https://www.briefasia.com/
articles.summary: South Korean Chipmakers Set for Strong 2027 on Memory Supply Crunch  https://www.briefasia.com/
articles.full_text:
Supply Tightness Persists into Year-End
The global memory market remains undersupplied heading into the final quarter of 2026, a condition driven primarily by continued capital deployment in artificial intelligence infrastructure. Data centre operators are absorbing high-bandwidth memory modules faster than manufacturers can scale output, creating pricing leverage for the two South Korean chip giants that dominate production.
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix together control more than 70 per cent of global DRAM capacity and roughly half of NAND Flash production. Both companies have reported that spot and contract negotiations for fourth-quarter deliveries reflect tightening availability, with lead times extending beyond historical norms. The undersupply environment marks a reversal from the inventory overhang that weighed on memory prices through much of 2024 and early 2025.
Industry data shows that contract prices for both DRAM and NAND Flash have climbed sequentially for three consecutive quarters. Samsung Electronics disclosed in its most recent earnings briefing that average selling prices for server DRAM rose by double-digit percentages quarter-on-quarter, while SK Hynix reported similar trajectories for its high-bandwidth memory products. The pricing momentum is expected to carry into the first half of 2027, barring a sharp pullback in data centre capital expenditure.
AI Infrastructure Drives Structural Shift
The memory shortage is not a cyclical blip but reflects structural changes in demand composition. Hyperscale cloud providers and enterprise AI labs are deploying large language models and machine learning workloads that require memory subsystems several times denser than traditional server configurations. High-bandwidth memory, particularly HBM3 and the forthcoming HBM3E variants, commands premium pricing and longer production cycles, leaving less capacity available for commodity DRAM.
SK Hynix has pivoted aggressively toward HBM, allocating more than half of its advanced fabrication capacity to these products. Samsung Electronics, while maintaining a broader portfolio, has similarly expanded HBM output and secured design wins with multiple hyperscale customers. Both companies are investing in new fabrication lines, but meaningful capacity additions are not expected until late 2027 or early 2028, prolonging the supply-demand imbalance.
NAND Flash is experiencing parallel dynamics. Data centre operators are upgrading storage arrays to support larger training datasets and inference workloads, driving demand for enterprise-grade SSDs. Consumer electronics, by contrast, remain sluggish; smartphone and PC shipments in Asia-Pacific markets have underperformed forecasts throughout 2026. The bifurcation means that memory manufacturers are prioritising higher-margin data centre products over consumer channels, further tightening availability in the former.
Price Ceiling from Long-Term Agreements
Despite favourable supply conditions, revenue upside for Samsung and SK Hynix faces constraints from contractual structures. A significant portion of memory sales to hyperscale customers is governed by long-term agreements that include price caps or formulaic escalation clauses. These contracts, typically spanning 12 to 24 months, were negotiated when memory prices were depressed and reflected customer efforts to lock in predictable costs.
As spot prices have risen above LTA ceilings, memory manufacturers have limited ability to capture full market pricing for contracted volumes. Samsung Electronics acknowledged in recent analyst calls that LTA provisions will dampen average selling price growth even as spot transactions command premiums. SK Hynix has indicated similar dynamics, noting that contract renewals scheduled for early 2027 will offer opportunities to reset pricing baselines, but current-year revenue will reflect older agreements.
The price cap mechanism also creates strategic tension. Hyperscale customers are hesitant to renegotiate terms mid-contract, fearing that concessions will erode their bargaining position in future cycles. Memory manufacturers, meanwhile, are reluctant to alienate key accounts by pushing too aggressively on price, given the concentrated nature of data centre demand. This standoff is likely to keep a lid on margin expansion in the near term, even as volume growth remains robust.
Regional Capacity and Geopolitical Considerations
South Korea's memory industry operates within a broader geopolitical context that influences investment decisions and supply chain configuration. Both Samsung and SK Hynix maintain the majority of their advanced fabrication capacity on the Korean peninsula, with some NAND production in China. Export controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment and technology transfer restrictions have complicated plans to expand Chinese operations, pushing new investment toward domestic sites or allied jurisdictions.
Japan and Taiwan have emerged as alternative locations for packaging and testing facilities, particularly for HBM products that require tight integration with logic dies. SK Hynix has established partnerships with TSMC for advanced packaging, while Samsung is expanding its own packaging capacity in South Korea. These moves reflect a strategic shift toward vertical integration and geographic diversification, reducing reliance on any single production node.
Southeast Asian markets, meanwhile, represent both a demand growth vector and a potential assembly hub. Singapore and Malaysia host significant data centre capacity, and memory manufacturers are exploring local partnerships to shorten logistics chains. However, advanced fabrication remains concentrated in Northeast Asia, and no immediate plans exist to transfer leading-edge DRAM or NAND production to the region.
Outlook and Market Positioning
Analyst consensus for 2027 points to high single-digit to low double-digit revenue growth for Samsung Electronics' semiconductor division and SK Hynix, driven primarily by memory products. Operating margin expansion is expected to be more modest, constrained by the factors outlined above. Both companies are also navigating the transition to next-generation process nodes, which entail higher capital intensity and longer ramp periods.
The consumer electronics recovery, if it materialises, could provide additional upside, but visibility remains limited. Smartphone demand in China has been weaker than anticipated, and PC refresh cycles tied to new operating system launches have not generated the expected memory content growth. For now, data centre infrastructure remains the dominant narrative, and memory manufacturers are aligning product roadmaps and capacity allocation accordingly.
Long-term, the memory market's centre of gravity is shifting toward AI and cloud infrastructure, a trend that favours suppliers with advanced technology portfolios and strong customer relationships. Samsung and SK Hynix are well positioned in this environment, but sustained leadership will require continued investment in R&D, process technology, and supply chain resilience. The next 18 months will test their ability to balance volume growth with pricing discipline in a market that rewards scale and technical differentiation in equal measure.

articles.title: A-Root Subsidiary NSRC to Supply Lithography Equipment to Taiwanese Power Semiconductor Maker, Entering AI Data Center Supply Chain - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: A-Root Subsidiary NSRC to Supply Lithography Equipment to Taiwanese Power Semiconductor Maker, Entering AI Data Center Supply Chain  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
NSRC, the semiconductor equipment subsidiary of South Korea's A-Root, has signed a lithography equipment supply contract with Taiwan's Company P, a comprehensive power semiconductor manufacturer, entering the global AI data center power infrastructure supply chain.
NSRC said on the 19th that it has won an order for lithography equipment to be installed at Company P's local production fab in Taiwan. Lithography equipment is core equipment in the semiconductor front-end process that uses light to etch fine circuit patterns onto wafers, and it determines a fab's yield and precision.
The customer, Company P, is a Taiwanese integrated device manufacturer (IDM) that produces MOSFETs, diodes, Schottky diodes, and insulated-gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs). The company's power semiconductors are supplied to large US AI data centers and used as core components in power conversion and distribution facilities, server cooling systems, and power supply units (PSUs). They are the foundational components that keep power supply, conversion, distribution, and cooling operating smoothly within data centers.
The contract is significant in that NSRC converted the technical expertise accumulated in South Korea's semiconductor equipment modification and refurbishment business, along with its network of overseas partners in the US, China, and Japan, into an actual overseas order. The company views its ability to handle the entire process — not just equipment procurement but also installation, verification, setup, and maintenance — as the competitive edge of its refurbishment business, and has recently hired a number of process and equipment engineers from major South Korean semiconductor companies such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
"With the spread of AI data centers, power supply and cooling efficiency have emerged as key challenges, and demand for power semiconductors and the equipment to produce them is rising rapidly," a company official said. "Through the lithography equipment order for Company P, we have entered the global AI data center value chain, and we expect orders for equipment related to AI data center power semiconductor manufacturing to expand in the second half of this year and into next year."
NSRC plans to use this order as a springboard to make a full-scale push into the power semiconductor equipment market. It expects that as AI data centers multiply, server power consumption will grow and power management will become more important, driving expanded production facility investment by power semiconductor makers. As power consumption and heat dissipation emerge as core challenges for AI infrastructure, new line expansions and process equipment orders from global power semiconductor companies are moving in tandem.
Meanwhile, A-Root, founded in September 2002, is a company engaged in the industrial printer and hardware manufacturing business, including POS printers and mobile label printers, and also operates an equipment distribution and refurbishment business through its semiconductor equipment subsidiary NSRC.

SK Hynix is partnering with the government, the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation, and commercial banks to support the strengthening of competitiveness and symbiotic development of semiconductor materials, components and equipment companies.
SK Hynix announced that it held an "Export Supply Chain Strengthening Guarantee" agreement ceremony and a first guarantee certificate handover ceremony on the 19th at the Yongin Cluster Promotion Center in the Yongin General Industrial Complex in Gyeonggi Province.
The Export Supply Chain Strengthening Guarantee is a financial program designed to support small and mid-sized semiconductor materials, components and equipment companies that are struggling to secure funding due to high interest rates and a global economic slowdown. SK Hynix and commercial banks contribute funds, while the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation provides guarantees, establishing a total financial support system of 2 trillion won.
Materials, components and equipment companies can benefit from expanded loan limits and preferential interest rates, as well as reduced guarantee fee burdens incurred during the lending process. On this day, a "First Guarantee Certificate Handover Ceremony" was also held for partner companies receiving support under the Export Supply Chain Strengthening Guarantee.
Prior to the agreement ceremony, SK Hynix President and CEO Kwak No-jung, Minister of Trade, Industry and Energy Kim Jung-gwan, representatives from the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation, four major commercial banks including KB Kookmin, Shinhan, Woori, and Hana Bank, and materials, components and equipment partner companies toured the construction site of SK Hynix's first fab (factory) at the Yongin Semiconductor Cluster and the development site of the "Trinity Fab." The Trinity Fab is an advanced semiconductor Yangsan-linked fab being built within the Yongin first fab through a joint investment of 870 billion won by the government, local governments, and SK Hynix.
The Trinity Fab provides an environment where the performance of technologies and products from materials, components and equipment companies can be tested and verified in advance to ensure they can be used without issues in actual production. Until now, domestic materials, components and equipment small and medium-sized enterprises have faced difficulties in commercialization because it was hard to test their independently developed new technologies and products in real semiconductor production environments. The Trinity Fab is expected to play a key role as a hub that resolves these challenges, enhancing the technological self-reliance of materials, components and equipment companies and significantly accelerating the domestication of advanced technologies and products.
During the meeting on this day, representatives from partner companies also conveyed field-level requests regarding the stabilization of the semiconductor supply chain and technological self-reliance. Participants agreed to strengthen symbiotic cooperation between large corporations and small and medium-sized enterprises to maintain the global competitiveness of "K-Semiconductors."
SK Hynix President and CEO Kwak No-jung stated, "To secure the global competitiveness of South Korea's semiconductor industry at a national level and further strengthen the standing of 'K-Semiconductors,' it is essential to build a robust materials, components and equipment ecosystem." He added, "Based on this export supply chain fund support and the creation of a one-stop technology verification environment through the Trinity Fab, we will join forces with our partners to further solidify our technological leadership in the global semiconductor market."

Shares of South Korea's Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell sharply in early trading on Oct. 19 before paring losses and attempting a rebound. The recent weakness in chip stocks is attributed in part to questions over whether Big Tech's data center spending will translate into actual profits. Rising U.S. Treasury yields, currency volatility and inflation concerns have also weighed on risk appetite. In a report, Lee Soo-rim, an analyst at DS Investment & Securities, said "the recent market plunge centered on semiconductors reflects a combination of interest rates, inflation, exchange rates and concerns over slowing AI investment," adding that "physical semiconductor demand remains strong, but the market is applying a higher discount rate to the sustainability of that demand."
Concerns over the rise of China's largest DRAM maker, ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), added to the losses. On Oct. 9, CXMT said it would launch a 4F² server DRAM within the year, cutting cell area by about 33% compared with the existing 6F² structure. Kevin Cassidy, an analyst at Rosenblatt, raised the possibility that CXMT's 4F² cell is a "paper tiger," noting that given CXMT's process technology, the cell could be about 34% larger than rivals' existing 6F² products. The view is that with earnings forecasts holding steady while valuations and supply-demand conditions have deteriorated simultaneously, the current situation could be a buying opportunity for medium-term investors.
Another supporting factor is that the earnings floor has risen compared with the past. Nvidia's push to co-design the base die for its in-house HBM, NVHBM, with Samsung Electronics and TSMC also supports the durability of HBM demand. articles.full_text:
Source：Getty Images
Taiwan plans to tighten restrictions on advanced AI chips and servers exported to China, bringing its regulations closer to those of the United States. The proposed measures could give Taiwanese authorities new powers to prosecute unauthorized shipments of sensitive AI hardware.

How Taiwan's New AI Chip Export Controls Could Affect China
By CommonWealth Magazine
web only
Taiwan is preparing to impose stricter export controls on advanced semiconductors and artificial intelligence servers destined for China, a move that could significantly change how the island regulates the international trade of high-performance computing equipment.
Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin confirmed in an October 12 interview with Bloomberg that the government plans to add AI servers and advanced semiconductors to its list of controlled export items.
Under the proposed framework, shipping restricted AI hardware to China without authorization could become a criminal offense under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act.
The government has not announced when the new restrictions will take effect.
The proposal represents a potentially significant development for Taiwan, which occupies a central position in the global AI hardware supply chain.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) manufactures advanced chips used by leading technology companies, while Taiwanese manufacturers play a major role in assembling AI servers for international customers.
The new restrictions could therefore affect not only chip shipments but also the movement of complete computing systems.
What AI chip export restrictions does Taiwan already have?
Taiwan already operates a strategic high-tech export control system, including controls on sensitive technologies and restrictions involving designated entities.
Companies exporting controlled products must comply with applicable licensing requirements and restrictions on prohibited destinations or end users.
Taiwan has also expanded restrictions involving certain Chinese technology companies, including Huawei and Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC).
However, these existing controls are not identical to the broader restrictions now being proposed.
The central issue is whether Taiwan can more directly regulate shipments of advanced AI hardware to China, including products that may be diverted through intermediaries.
The proposed measures would strengthen the domestic legal framework for controlling certain shipments.
They should not be interpreted as a blanket ban on every semiconductor or server exported to China.
The exact product categories, technical thresholds, licensing exemptions, and enforcement procedures will depend on the final regulations.
What is Taiwan planning to change?
According to Kung, Taiwan intends to add advanced AI servers and cutting-edge semiconductors to its controlled export list.
The measures are intended to align more closely with restrictions imposed by the United States.
Washington has limited China's access to certain advanced AI accelerators and semiconductor technologies on national security grounds.
Taiwan's proposed changes could make it harder for companies to use Taiwanese manufacturing and export channels to circumvent those restrictions.
Crucially, the government is also seeking stronger domestic enforcement powers.
Under the proposed framework, unauthorized exports of newly controlled AI hardware could be prosecuted directly under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act.
That would differ from situations in which authorities must rely on other existing legal provisions to investigate suspected smuggling or misrepresentation.
However, criminal liability would depend on the final legal framework, the goods involved, and the specific conduct.
Why does the United States want Taiwan to tighten export controls?
The United States has sought to restrict China's access to advanced computing hardware that could support military applications, intelligence operations, and sophisticated artificial intelligence systems.
But export controls become less effective when restricted products can be purchased through intermediaries or redirected through international supply chains.
Taiwan is especially important because of its role in semiconductor manufacturing and AI server assembly.
Even when a chip is designed by an American company, its production, packaging, integration, or final system assembly may involve Taiwanese businesses.
That creates a need for coordination across jurisdictions.
In his October interview, Kung linked Taiwan's planned adjustments to commitments made under the 2026 US–Taiwan trade agreement.
Closer coordination could reduce differences between the two countries' regulatory systems, although the precise scope of the Taiwanese measures remains to be announced.
How could the restrictions affect Nvidia and Taiwan's AI server manufacturers?
The potential impact depends on the products covered and the destination of shipments.
Nvidia designs AI accelerators that are manufactured through a global supply chain involving TSMC and other partners.
Taiwanese manufacturers also assemble complete servers incorporating these processors.
A restriction covering only certain semiconductor products would have a different effect from one covering finished AI servers.
For example, a complete server may contain multiple accelerators, memory, networking components, and supporting hardware.
Regulating finished systems could reduce opportunities to circumvent chip-specific restrictions by exporting assembled equipment.
Manufacturers would need to evaluate product classifications, customer identities, ultimate end users, and licensing obligations.
However, it would be premature to estimate the financial impact on individual companies before the government publishes the controlled-item definitions.
Why has AI chip smuggling become a major issue?
Advanced AI accelerators are expensive and strategically important products.
Restrictions on their sale to China have created incentives for unauthorized resale, diversion, and complex procurement arrangements.
Authorities in several jurisdictions have investigated suspected attempts to move restricted computing equipment through intermediaries.
For Taiwan, the challenge is particularly sensitive because of the concentration of semiconductor manufacturing and AI server assembly on the island.
The issue also raises questions about the responsibilities of manufacturers, distributors, logistics providers, and overseas customers.
Existing CommonWealth reporting on the Supermicro AI hardware controversy examined how international trade restrictions can intersect with Taiwan's technology supply chains.
The proposed export-control changes would give Taiwanese authorities an additional policy instrument to address such risks.
Could Taiwan's new rules stop China from obtaining advanced AI chips?
Stricter controls could make unauthorized shipments more difficult and increase the legal risks for participants.
However, export restrictions alone cannot guarantee that prohibited hardware will never reach China.
Their effectiveness depends on enforcement, international cooperation, product traceability, and the ability to identify indirect shipments.
The final impact will also depend on whether the new regulations cover individual chips, assembled servers, or both.
For Taiwan, the challenge is to strengthen compliance without unnecessarily disrupting legitimate technology trade.
FAQs
Has Taiwan banned AI chip exports to China?
No blanket ban has been established by the announced proposal. Taiwan already has controls on certain sensitive products and entities, and the government plans to expand restrictions on advanced AI hardware.
When will Taiwan's new AI chip export controls take effect?
As of October 19, 2026, the government has not announced an implementation date.
Which AI chips will be restricted?
The government has indicated that advanced semiconductors and AI servers will be included. Detailed technical specifications and product classifications have not yet been announced.
Will exporting AI chips to China become a criminal offense?
Unauthorized exports of products covered by the proposed new controls could become subject to criminal prosecution under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act once the measures take effect. This does not mean every chip export to China would be illegal.
Will the restrictions affect TSMC?
They could affect compliance requirements for relevant products and transactions involving Taiwan's semiconductor supply chain. The direct implications will depend on the final rules and existing contractual and regulatory arrangements.
Are Taiwan's export controls the same as those of the United States?
No. Taiwan and the United States operate separate legal systems. Taiwan is seeking closer alignment, but companies must evaluate their obligations under each applicable jurisdiction.
The Bottom Line
Taiwan's planned AI export controls are significant because they could close a gap between the island's central role in manufacturing advanced computing hardware and its ability to enforce restrictions on unauthorized shipments.
But the measures remain a proposal until the government publishes and implements the relevant regulations.
For companies operating across Taiwan, China, and the United States, the most important questions are which products will be covered, what licenses will be required, and how the new rules will be enforced.
Policy status: October 19, 2026. The proposed expansion of export controls has been publicly confirmed, but the implementation date and complete product coverage have not been announced.

articles.full_text:
South Korea's Hanmi Semiconductor has established a local subsidiary, Hanmi USA, in San Jose, California, accelerating its push into the artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor advanced packaging equipment market. The company is seen as having secured a local technical support base just as U.S. investment in semiconductor production facilities spreads beyond memory and foundry into advanced packaging.
Hanmi Semiconductor said on the 19th that it held an opening ceremony on the 16th (local time) at the Hanmi USA office in San Jose. The event was attended by Chairman Kwak Dong-shin and other key executives and employees. With the establishment of this subsidiary, the company now has its fourth overseas base, following Taiwan, China, and Singapore, with the U.S. added.
Hanmi USA will use Silicon Valley — home to global semiconductor companies and Big Tech firms — as an integrated operating hub for its U.S. business. The plan is to deploy experienced engineers locally in step with the startup schedules of new U.S. semiconductor plants and to proactively provide technical support including equipment installation, operation, and maintenance. The company explained that the core purpose of establishing the subsidiary is to build a close-response system with local customers.
The expansion dovetails with the rapid buildout of U.S. semiconductor production capacity. As memory and foundry plant expansions continue, demand for advanced packaging equipment is bound to rise as well.

|---|---|
| SK Hynix | Broke ground on HBM packaging plant in West Lafayette, Indiana (August 2025), targeting operation in the second half of 2028 | 
| Micron | Building new memory plant in Boise, Idaho; broke ground on $100 billion production facility in Clay, New York | 
| Intel | Began 18A (1.8nm-class) process and advanced packaging production at Chandler, Arizona plant | 
| Amkor Technology | Building advanced packaging and test facility in Peoria, Arizona; expanded investment plan to $12 billion | 
Note: Amkor Technology's first production facility is scheduled to begin operation in early 2028, and Micron aims to produce DRAM and HBM at its Boise plant.
Tesla's in-house semiconductor production project "Terafab" is also cited as a variable. Taiwan's TSMC, the world's largest foundry, said on the 15th that it is discussing the possibility of participating in Terafab. The broader the U.S. manufacturing base becomes, the larger the pie for the back-end equipment market that Hanmi Semiconductor is targeting. However, specific order volumes by U.S. customer related to this subsidiary's establishment were not disclosed.
Hanmi Semiconductor holds the No. 1 global market share in thermal compression (TC) bonders, a key piece of equipment in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) manufacturing. A TC bonder is equipment that bonds multiple DRAM chips using heat and pressure to produce HBM. Recently, the company has been supplying three types of 2.5D TC bonders (40C2S, 40C2W, 120) and two types of 2.5D flip-chip (FC) bonders (FCB 3.5, FCB 75) used in AI semiconductor packaging to foundries and outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) companies. It has also expanded its business areas to include the "BOC COB bonder" for high-spec memory production and the "EMI shield," which blocks electromagnetic interference. The company said it has also risen to No. 1 in the world in the micro saw and vision placement (MSVP) equipment market.
The establishment of the subsidiary is also symbolic in that it comes 46 years after the company's founding. The late founder and chairman Kwak No-kwon worked at U.S.-based Motorola for 14 years starting in 1967 before founding Hanmi Semiconductor in South Korea in 1980. The company name "Hanmi" — combining the Korean words for Korea and the U.S. — reflects the founder's intention to serve as a bridge connecting the semiconductor industries of South Korea and the United States. The company emphasized that the founding vision has become a reality with the establishment of the U.S. subsidiary.
"The United States is a key market leading the global AI industry and advanced semiconductor technology," Chairman Kwak Dong-shin said. "Hanmi USA will provide close technical support to local U.S. customers and expand cooperation with global semiconductor companies to further strengthen our competitiveness in the global market."
Meanwhile, Hanmi Semiconductor's earnings outlook is also bright, driven by recovering TC bonder demand as the HBM market transitions to HBM4. According to financial information provider FnGuide, the consensus for Hanmi Semiconductor's third-quarter results (average of securities firm estimates) is 263.7 billion won (approximately $198.3 million) in revenue and 129.1 billion won (approximately $97.1 million) in operating profit. That is up 58.6% and 90.4%, respectively, from the same period last year, with an expected operating margin of 49.0%.

The market views the U.S. subsidiary as meaningful for expanding mid- to long-term customer touchpoints rather than for short-term results, since demand for equipment installation and technical support could surge after 2027–2028, when new U.S. fabs begin full operation. However, cost burdens from operating the local subsidiary and the timing of confirmed orders by U.S. customer remain variables. Hanmi Semiconductor plans to build its local technical support system in stages and broaden the scope of cooperation with global customers.

The Bank of Japan faces pressure to raise interest rates again as inflation picks up. But the weak factory output could make the bank wait. The high oil prices and weak yen add to the costs of imports and squeeze household spending. The market now waits for the inflation report for Japan on October 23, ahead of the BOJ’s October 29-30 meeting. In my view, the pause in October would still leave room for the hike in December. This article discusses the key economic drivers and technical levels that could shape the next move in USDJPY, EURJPY and GBPJPY.
BOJ Interest Rate Forecast: Inflation and Growth Shape the Next Hike
Ueda Signals More BOJ Rate Hikes as Oil Nears $110
In the speech delivered by Deputy Governor Shinichi Uchida, Ueda said that the Japanese economy continued to recover moderately. The strong global demand for AI helped exports return to growth, while high corporate profits supported investment.
Household spending remained resilient as the conditions of employment and income improved. The steady economy gives the BOJ more room to raise borrowing costs without sharply weakening demand.
The same speech warned that firms continued to pass higher costs for input and wages into consumer prices. Ueda said that underlying inflation was approaching 2% while financial conditions remained supportive after the increase in interest rates in September. The BOJ is now more worried that inflation could increase further.
The IMF reinforced that message in an interview reported on October 17. Asia and Pacific director Krishna Srinivasan said that the BOJ may need to tighten faster if inflation increases more than expected. The rising energy prices further add to that risk.
Brent crude oil reached near the $110 level last week. The high oil prices and a weak yen raise the import costs for Japan. They can also squeeze household spending and company margins. This makes the pace of tightening harder to judge.
US Treasury Undersecretary Erin Browne said that Japan’s monetary policy and currency should reflect the shift away from deflation. She also warned that sharp moves by the currency could force investors to unwind positions and raise financing costs. These comments add to the scrutiny of yen weakness.
Japan Inflation and Factory Data Test the BOJ Outlook
Core inflation in Tokyo increased to 2.7% in September from 1.8% in August. That sharp increase gives the BOJ another reason to watch pressures on prices closely.
National core inflation is also expected to increase. The inflation data for Japan is due on October 23. A confirmed increase in national inflation would strengthen the case for another rate hike.
The latest activity data show that the BOJ may still move slowly. The chart below shows that the core machinery orders increased 5.2% in August from the previous month. This data beats the forecast for a 3% increase and reversed July’s 3.7% drop.
But the revised industrial production dropped 2.4% in August, compared with the initial estimate of a decline of 1.7%. The strong orders point to better demand for equipment, but the drop in output shows that the manufacturers still face pressure. This gives the BOJ a reason to check whether investment demand turns into stronger production before raising rates again.
USDJPY Forecast: Break Above 159 Could Open the Way to 160
The chart below shows a big gap between the 10-year Treasury yields for the US and Japan. The gap of more than 2% still favors dollar assets. But the US dollar corrected lower on Friday towards the key support of 101.80. In my view, USD/JPY could weaken if US yields fall further or the BOJ signals an earlier increase. But the BOJ pause in October and renewed expectations of Fed tightening could support the pair.
From a technical perspective, USDJPY produced a strong rebound in September from the long-term support at 153. This support is highlighted by the ascending broadening wedge pattern that stretches from the April 2025 lows.
This rebound has pushed the pair towards the key resistance in the 160 area. Last week’s candle was a little muted, and if the pair continues to trade above the 159 level, it will move towards the 160 area. articles.title: IMF Executive Director: "South Korea Is the Only Advanced Economy Expanding Fiscal Space… AI Boom Should Be Viewed Long-Term" - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: IMF Executive Director: "South Korea Is the Only Advanced Economy Expanding Fiscal Space… AI Boom Should Be Viewed Long-Term"  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Choi Ji-young, the executive director representing South Korea at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), met with reporters during the IMF-World Bank (WB) annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, and assessed that South Korea is the only advanced economy expanding its fiscal space. She relayed that positive mentions of South Korea within the IMF board have become unusually frequent.
At a press briefing on the 15th (local time), Choi said, "Among advanced economies right now, South Korea is the only country where policy space is growing," adding, "There is a shared consensus among IMF staff that South Korea needs to make investments that can boost its growth potential in the current environment, and I agree with that view."
She explained that while major advanced economies face austerity pressures due to the global economic slowdown and deteriorating fiscal soundness, South Korea is simultaneously seeing improvements in its growth outlook and fiscal space thanks to the semiconductor boom. As a result, she added, the phrase "especially South Korea" repeatedly comes up whenever the World Economic Outlook (WEO) or the Regional Economic Outlook (REO) for Asia-Pacific is presented to the IMF board.
Choi said, "Other advanced economies are in very poor shape, but South Korea is the only one seeing rising growth rates and AI-related benefits that are larger than expected," adding, "The mood on the IMF board is one of great envy toward South Korea." She went on to describe South Korea's situation as "so different from other advanced economies that it stands apart on its own — a case of positive isolation."
IMF Assesses Next Year's Budget Proposal as Neutral in Stance
Choi relayed that the IMF internally assesses the South Korean government's budget proposal for next year as a neutral fiscal stance, leaning neither toward expansion nor austerity. This contrasts with the ongoing domestic political debate in South Korea over "expansionary fiscal policy" versus "fiscal soundness," sparked by the government's 2027 budget proposal setting total expenditure at 820.9 trillion won (approximately $617.4 billion), a 12.8% increase from the previous year and the largest on record.
She explained, "Government revenue is rising sharply, while the spending growth rate is 12.8%, and with some debt being repaid and a substantial portion being saved into the Future Response Fund, it can be viewed as slightly contractionary in some respects."
She particularly noted the structure of the newly established Future Response Fund, totaling 162.3 trillion won (approximately $122.1 billion), of which 104 trillion won (approximately $78.2 billion) will not be spent immediately but managed as surplus funds. Choi said, "A portion will be spent in next year's budget, but roughly 60% is structured to be saved," adding, "That in itself is positive."
She pointed out that channeling all of the sharply increased tax revenue into debt repayment is not necessarily rational fiscal management. "If a company suddenly sees a surge in profits, is it necessarily rational financial management to pay off all its debt and reduce leverage to zero?" she asked. "The company should be making investments that allow it to grow further and increase market share going forward. There is a consensus on that point."
Focus Should Be on Growth and Innovation Investment, Not the Debt-to-GDP Ratio
In its Fiscal Monitor report released this month, the IMF projected South Korea's general government debt-to-GDP ratio at 47.3% for this year. That is 7.1 percentage points lower than the 54.4% forecast in April.
Choi expressed the view that rather than obsessing over the government debt-to-GDP ratio itself, attention should be paid to economic growth and innovation investment. "In a case like South Korea, where the national debt is around 50% of GDP — a reasonably sound level — the debt-to-GDP ratio can shift dramatically depending on how well the economy grows," she said. "Rather than viewing the debt-to-GDP ratio too rigidly, what matters more is how much we invest in innovation and how much we grow going forward."
She also raised the possibility that the growth-potential-enhancing effects of the Future Response Fund and other measures may not be fully reflected in the IMF's current projections. "The portion of growth-rate increases driven by policy factors does not appear to be reflected in the growth forecast data the IMF has published," she said. "In that respect, it could be seen as somewhat conservative." She added, "If those factors continue to be reflected going forward, I think things could move in a more positive direction."
AI Boom Downturn Could Deliver a Major Shock… But Take the Long View
Choi warned that since South Korea benefits greatly from the AI boom, the shock could also be significant if the investment cycle turns. "In South Korea's case, if the AI boom fizzles out, there would be major adjustments in the stock market and the current account balance, along with significant negative impacts on corporations," she said. "There could clearly be a shock on the growth front as well."
However, she relayed that there is a view within the IMF that AI investment will continue for a considerable period. "Most of the AI investment happening right now is in data centers, and data center construction can take about 10 years," she explained. "Investment is just getting started now, and I don't think it will suddenly collapse in a couple of years and become meaningless."
Regarding the recent sharp stock-price volatility of AI-related companies, she advised, "Given that there is an internal view that AI investment itself will continue for a considerable period, it's better to take a long-term perspective rather than overreacting to short-term stock-price fluctuations."
She added, however, that the IMF's own view of AI is not favorable. "Fundamentally, it is not favorable," she said. "The view is that rather than productivity gains materializing rapidly in the short term, the negative impact on the labor market is likely to be significant."
She also stressed that fiscal policy should focus on targeted support for vulnerable groups. Choi said, "The AI supercycle itself is not necessarily a result of fiscal policy," but added, "In the unexpected Middle East conflict situation, the government responded appropriately and played a role in smoothing out the pain felt by citizens and businesses." She continued, "The assessment of fiscal policy and the government's role so far has been positive," but added, "The IMF continues to emphasize that fiscal support itself should be temporary and targeted selectively at vulnerable groups who truly need it."

articles.full_text:
▲ Choi Ji-young, Executive Director at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), speaks with a South Korean press corps at a restaurant in Bangkok, Thailand, on October 15 (local time).
Choi Ji-young, Executive Director at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), stated, "While other countries are seeing their fiscal space shrink, South Korea is the only one whose fiscal space has expanded (thanks to the semiconductor boom)."
Visiting Bangkok, Thailand, to attend the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, Executive Director Choi met with the South Korean press corps on October 15 (local time) and remarked, "The situation is so different from other advanced economies that South Korea stands alone, detached from IMF discussions," describing it as a "positive isolation."
According to the World Economic Outlook released just ahead of the annual meetings, the IMF projected South Korea's real gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate for this year at 3.3%.
This is an upward revision of 0.7 percentage points in just three months compared to the growth forecast of 2.6% announced in July.
It is also higher than this year's global economic growth forecast of 3.1%.
Choi explained, "This is the first time since 2016 (excluding 2020 when COVID-19 broke out) that our country's growth rate has surpassed the global growth rate," adding, "Amid mounting negative pressures on the global economy due to the Middle East situation, the Russia-Ukraine war, and trade tensions between nations, only our country has shown a (clear) increase in growth rate."
Furthermore, regarding the IMF's growth forecast for South Korea this year, she noted, "It does not seem to reflect (the government's) investment in growth potential," adding, "In that respect, it can be considered somewhat conservative (in its prediction)."
Choi diagnosed that with South Korea being a rare exception in performing well economically, the policy advice typically given by the IMF no longer fits South Korea's situation.
She added, "The IMF's basic policy advice is that because there is generalized inflation due to tariff issues and rising oil prices, and things could worsen going forward, fiscal and monetary policies should generally be tightened," noting that "this general advice itself no longer fits South Korea."
Instead, Choi explained, "What the IMF discusses (regarding South Korea) is growth potential," and "The shared consensus (within the IMF) is that while other countries lack the capacity to foster growth potential, South Korea (has that capacity and) must continue making investments to expand its growth potential."
Regarding South Korea's budget bill for next year, she said, "Krishna Srinivasan, Director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, views it neutrally," pointing out that "while fiscal revenues (total revenue) are increasing significantly, the growth rate of fiscal expenditures (total expenditure) is (lower at) 12.8%."
She further noted, "Some of it is used to repay government bonds, and a significant portion is accumulated into the Future Response Fund," adding, "In a way, (next year's budget bill) also has some tightening aspects."
Addressing the criticism that South Korea's fiscal policy is expansionary while its monetary policy is restrictive, creating a policy mismatch, Choi drew a line, stating, "Regarding the claim that fiscal policy is expansionary, Srinivasan, the Director of the Asia and Pacific Department, stated that he does not view (South Korea's fiscal policy) as expansionary."
Her stance is that it is not desirable to use all additional tax revenues solely to repay government bonds, contrary to some arguments.
Choi remarked, "Wouldn't it be unreasonable financial management for a company to pay off all its debts just because its revenue suddenly increased?" and added, "There is a consensus that we must continue to make investments that enable companies to grow further and expand their market share."
In this context, she explained that the IMF views the newly established Future Response Fund positively.
Choi noted, "From the IMF's perspective, we must examine the (specific) details," while evaluating that "the structure of accumulating a portion of next year's expenditures, about 60%, is positive."
She added, "When the annual consultations begin in November, that topic will likely be raised from the IMF's side."
She also conveyed that the IMF's perspective is that the artificial intelligence (AI) investment boom will continue for a considerable period.
Choi stated, "Most of the heavy AI investments happening right now are in data centers, and building a data center can take about 10 years," adding, "We do not believe that investments happening right now will suddenly collapse the year after next and become meaningless."
She added, "There will be volatility, just like U.S. AI company stocks dropping (today), but we need to look at the big picture over the long term."
However, regarding the IMF's view on AI, she said, "Fundamentally, it is not favorable," and "We believe that rather than bringing short-term productivity improvements, AI is likely to have a significant negative impact on the labor market."
She also explained that the national debt ratio should be lowered by expanding growth, which serves as the denominator.
Previously, the IMF projected South Korea's general government debt (D2) to GDP ratio at 54.4% for this year and 56.6% for next year.
However, in this month's revised outlook, those ratios were lowered to 47.3% for this year and 46.2% for next year.
Choi explained, "When the national debt ratio is around 50% of GDP like in South Korea, the ratio varies drastically depending on how much growth is achieved."
She emphasized, "For a growing country like South Korea, rather than obsessing over the national debt ratio itself, it is important to focus on how much we invest in innovative areas and grow moving forward."
When asked whether the improvement in the debt ratio could be seen as the result of active fiscal policy, she drew a line, stating, "The AI supercycle itself did not come about as a result of fiscal policy."
However, she explained, "The IMF's position is that there was an unexpected Middle East conflict, and if the government had not played its proper role in that situation, the lives of the citizens would have been much worse."
She added, "In that respect, South Korea responded well from a fiscal standpoint (including the oil pricing system)."

articles.title: Japan Clears TSMC Kumamoto for 3nm Chip Production; EUV Scarcity Caps Output at 6,000 Wafers - Tech Times
articles.summary: Japan Clears TSMC Kumamoto for 3nm Chip Production; EUV Scarcity Caps Output at 6,000 Wafers  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry formally approved a revised production plan for TSMC's second fabrication plant in Kumamoto Prefecture on October 16, 2026, certifying what will become Japan's first facility capable of manufacturing 3-nanometer logic semiconductors. The approval is a genuine milestone — but the story behind the numbers is more technically revealing than the headline suggests. The original plan called for 48,000 wafers per month at 6nm and 12nm. The approved plan calls for 6,000 wafers per month at 3nm. That 87.5% capacity reduction is not a setback. It is a direct consequence of what 3nm manufacturing actually requires — and of who makes the equipment that enables it.
Japan's Node Upgrade — and the Volume Reckoning It Reveals
When TSMC first laid out plans for the Kumamoto second fab in February 2024, the blueprint called for producing 6nm and 12nm chips at a monthly capacity of 48,000 wafers, according to the JASM second fab announced in 2024 — a volume-first approach geared largely toward Japan's automotive and industrial sectors. Under the now-approved plan, the facility will produce 3nm chips at an initial monthly target of just 6,000 wafers, an 87.5% reduction in output volume compared to the prior design. METI approved the plan change on October 16.
The reduction is not a sign of diminished ambition. It reflects what happens when a facility moves from mature-node mass production into frontier-node manufacturing. At 3nm, a chip requires extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography — a technology that prints circuits with light at a wavelength of just 13.5 nanometers (0.000000053 inches), roughly one-fifteenth of a wavelength of visible light. EUV lithography is used on more than 20 critical layers at the 3nm node, compared to approximately 14 layers at 5nm. And only one company in the world is the sole manufacturer of EUV systems at commercial scale: ASML, the Dutch equipment maker.
TSMC and METI framed the revised plan explicitly around the requirements of 3nm manufacturing, which demands EUV equipment and carries a significantly heavier investment burden per wafer than the more mature nodes it replaces. METI's Director of the Information Industry Division, Tomonari Nanbu told reporters that "given the progress of AI transformation, 3nm cutting-edge logic semiconductors that power AI are indispensable," signaling that the ministry views the node upgrade as a strategic necessity.
TSMC has indicated that the 6,000-wafer figure represents only the first phase, and that production capacity will expand depending on the level of additional government support it receives.
Why EUV Scarcity — Not Strategy — Governs the Capacity Figure
Understanding why the Kumamoto II fab will start at 6,000 wafers per month instead of 48,000 requires understanding EUV tool availability.
ASML's EUV systems — the NXE series, which uses an optical system with a numerical aperture of 0.33 — are the workhorses of every advanced-node fab in the world. Each machine uses EUV plasma generation technology in which a pulsed laser fires at liquid tin droplets more than 50,000 times per second, producing photons at the 13.5nm wavelength that then pass through a reflective optical system to print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers.
ASML produces roughly 50 to 60 EUV systems per year globally. Every major foundry — TSMC in Taiwan and Arizona, Samsung in South Korea, Intel in the United States, and now Rapidus in Hokkaido — competes for allocation from that limited production line. Each EUV tool costs in excess of $150 million; installing and qualifying a single tool at a new fab takes months. A 3nm production line requires multiple such tools running in concert.
The 6,000-wafer-per-month figure represents what EUV tool allocation and yield ramp-up can realistically support at a new Japanese site in the 2026–2028 installation window, given that TSMC is simultaneously prioritizing equipment for its Fab 21 Phase 2 in Arizona (targeting 3nm production in the second half of 2027) and its continued 3nm and 2nm expansion in Taiwan. There was earlier reporting of a 15,000-wafer monthly figure when Taiwan approved the 3nm investment in March 2026; the official METI-certified plan lists 6,000 wafers per month. METI's official documents do not explain the difference, but the discrepancy is consistent with a first-phase ceiling set by tool availability rather than demand.
METI is explicitly considering increasing its support, and METI included the subsidy request in its fiscal year 2027 preliminary budget — a process that will determine whether TSMC can raise the 6,000-wafer ceiling before mass production begins in December 2028.
Subsidy Structure and Investment Scale
METI designated the Kumamoto II plant as a subsidy recipient under Japan's semiconductor reindustrialization program. The government originally planned to provide ¥732 billion (approximately $4.6 billion) in subsidies tied to the prior 6nm/12nm plan. With the revised blueprint now approved, that figure has been adjusted to ¥645.15 billion (approximately $4.1 billion), reflecting the reduced initial production volume, as documented in the METI official revised plan document.
The first Kumamoto fab's subsidy was also revised downward — from ¥476 billion to ¥409.5 billion (approximately $2.6 billion). Between the two plants, total committed public support fell from ¥1.208 trillion to ¥1.055 trillion (approximately $6.7 billion). However, METI is considering increasing the second fab's support as the full scale of the 3nm investment becomes clearer. TSMC's own statement confirmed total Kumamoto capital spending exceeds $23 billion (approximately ¥3.63 trillion) across both facilities.
Timeline: December 2028
Commercial production at the second Kumamoto fab is targeted for December 2028. Under METI's certification conditions, JASM commits to ten-year operation and to increasing production in the event of a domestic shortage — conditions attached to all Japanese government semiconductor subsidies.
The 2028 production date means Kumamoto's 3nm node will come online approximately one year after TSMC's 3nm capacity at its second Arizona fab, where Arizona 3nm production targets 2027 in the second half. That sequence reflects TSMC's global capital allocation priorities — Taiwan first, then Arizona under US CHIPS Act pressure, then Japan — rather than any deficiency in the Japanese site itself.
Kumamoto I Also Revised
METI's October 16 approval package extended to the existing Kumamoto I plant as well. Originally planned to run both 12–16nm and 22–28nm processes at a combined 55,000 wafers per month, the first fab plan revised to 22-28nm phases out all 12–16nm production, concentrating the facility on 22–28nm nodes (plus 40nm processes reserved for Japanese domestic customers) at 45,000 wafers per month across the subsidized facility footprint, and 50,000 wafers per month across the full plant.
JASM attributes this revision to how automotive and industrial customer demand has evolved — an implicit acknowledgment that sluggish electric vehicle adoption has moderated demand for the advanced-mature nodes originally planned for Kumamoto I. The move effectively repositions Kumamoto I as a stable-node workhorse for Sony image sensors, automotive chips, and industrial electronics, freeing the second facility to serve as the campus's leading-edge AI-oriented anchor.
The first fab has been operating since late 2024, when volume production began at 12–28nm. Its resilience was tested on July 28, 2026, when a magnitude 7.1 earthquake halted JASM Fab 1 operations for equipment inspections. The facility recorded a maximum seismic intensity of 5 at the fab site; analysts estimated a one-week shutdown could represent approximately $14 million in potential lost revenue, according to the TSMC Kumamoto earthquake impact estimate. The fab subsequently returned to normal operations.
What 3nm Means: Density, Power, and Why Artificial Intelligence Drives It
A 3nm chip is not merely a faster version of a 6nm chip. The performance gap is structural. TSMC's N3 process delivers 70% logic density over 5nm, plus a 15% performance improvement at the same transistor count, and a 30% reduction in power consumption compared to its 5nm node — the previous generation widely used in high-performance AI chips.
For AI workloads — the inference and training pipelines that power large language models, image generators, and autonomous systems — transistor density and power efficiency are the primary engineering constraints. More transistors per square millimeter means more compute per die; lower power per transistor means larger dies can be built without exceeding thermal limits. The combination makes 3nm the node at which AI accelerators cross from constrained to capable at the scale AI infrastructure requires.
TSMC CEO C.C. Wei met Prime Minister Takaichi in Tokyo in February 2026 to signal the shift in direction, citing "strong demand driven by AI" as the driving rationale for moving the second Kumamoto fab from 6nm to 3nm. Japan's PM Office stated that "there is a huge significance to have the world's most advanced semiconductor factory in Japan from the perspective of economic security."
By installing 3nm capacity in Japan, TSMC can serve GPU and AI accelerator customers who require geographically diversified supply chains, while also positioning the facility to capture Japanese hyperscaler and defense-adjacent demand. JASM's ownership structure — TSMC holds 86.5% of JASM with Sony Semiconductor Solutions at 6%, Denso at 5.5%, and Toyota at approximately 2% — ensures that Japan's largest technology, automotive, and electronics companies have direct investment stakes in the outcome.
