articles.title: Commentary: Across the Yalu, China pours concrete over North Korean sanctions - CNA
articles.summary: Commentary: Across the Yalu, China pours concrete over North Korean sanctions  CNA
articles.full_text:
A 12-year monument to mistrust, the China-North Korea bridge is open – locking in Beijing’s edge over Moscow and Washington, says this academic.
BOSTON, Massachusetts: For 12 years, the New Yalu River Bridge stood as the most expensive dead end in Northeast Asia. Completed by China in 2014 at a cost of US$350 million, the sleek four-lane cable-stayed span stretched across the border from Dandong only to terminate abruptly in unpaved North Korean farmland outside Sinuiju.
Now, after more than a decade of false starts, Beijing and Pyongyang officially opened the crossing to traffic on Oct 15.
Why open a 12-year-old bridge now? The answer goes well beyond border logistics. By turning on the tap of high-capacity commercial traffic, Beijing is physically retiring the era of sanctions-led pressure on North Korea – and ensuring that neither Moscow’s wartime courtship nor Washington’s appetite for fresh summiteering dilutes China’s position as the indispensable arbiter on the Korean Peninsula.
For a decade, the dormant bridge served as a barometer of quiet friction between the two socialist neighbours. After China finished the main span in 2014, disputes over who would pay for the North Korean customs complex and entry roads stalled the project.
Then came Pyongyang’s escalating nuclear tests, Beijing’s decision to back harsh United Nations Security Council sanctions in 2017, and finally Kim Jong-un’s draconian pandemic-era border closure. Opening a four-lane trade artery while the UN sanctions regime was at its peak would have been diplomatically awkward for Beijing and quarantined by Pyongyang.
That calculus has now inverted. Beijing has already dropped the word “denuclearisation” from its public diplomacy with Pyongyang, shifting from viewing North Korea’s nuclear arsenal as a proliferation liability to treating it as a durable buffer that ties down American military attention.
Once Beijing accepted a nuclear-armed North Korea as a baseline reality, keeping its primary commercial artery padlocked no longer made strategic sense.
The opening is the culmination of a methodical normalisation: cross-border truck freight resumed in 2023, the Beijing-Pyongyang passenger train restarted in March 2026 after a six-year suspension, and now the ageing single-lane Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge – built by Imperial Japan in 1937 – is being supplemented by a modern highway designed for heavy containerised freight.
THE RUSSIA CARD
Yet timing in Northeast Asia is never accidental, and two popular misreadings of this moment deserve to be challenged.
The first is the widespread notion that Kim Jong-un successfully used his high-profile military partnership with Vladimir Putin to strong-arm a reluctant China into re-engaging.
On the surface, the optics are seductive. Just five weeks ago, on Sep 7, North Korea and Russia inaugurated their first road bridge across the Tumen River, a project that raced from groundbreaking in April 2025 to ribbon-cutting in roughly 16 months.
Compared with China’s 12-year delay on the Yalu, Moscow’s sprint looked like a triumph of wartime expediency.
But optics should not be confused with economic gravity. China still accounts for over 98 per cent of North Korea’s official external trade. That single figure remains the defining reality of Pyongyang’s external relations – regardless of how “deep and close” its booming alignment with Moscow may appear to outside observers.
Moscow can supply Pyongyang with immediate security assurances, fuel, grain, and battlefield technologies in exchange for munitions and troops. What Russia’s sparsely populated Far East cannot provide is the industrial supply chain, consumer goods, agricultural inputs, and commercial scale that keep the North Korean economy functioning.
The “Russia card” certainly gave Kim the breathing room to negotiate with Beijing from a position of confidence rather than desperation. In the end, though, geography and scale bring Pyongyang back to the Yalu. By opening the bridge five weeks after the Tumen crossing, Beijing is reminding both Pyongyang and the world where the Peninsula’s real economic lifeline lies.
Once Beijing accepted a nuclear-armed North Korea as a baseline reality, keeping its primary commercial artery padlocked no longer made strategic sense.
NO THREE-WAY MILITARY PACT
The second misconception is that twin bridge openings with Russia and China within five weeks prove that a formal, monolithic Beijing-Moscow-Pyongyang bloc has locked into place. In reality, Beijing is moving to protect its bilateral leverage precisely because its horizon differs from Moscow’s.
Russia and North Korea are currently bound by urgent, transactional wartime needs, making both capitals comfortable with visible geopolitical disruption. Beijing’s priorities are fundamentally different.
As a global trading power deeply integrated into international markets, China wants a stable buffer state in Pyongyang and a resilient partner in Moscow, but it prefers to manage its relations with both on separate bilateral tracks rather than appearing to endorse a formal trilateral axis that could invite secondary sanctions or harden allied counter-coalitions.
Revitalising Liaoning province – for which Dandong is the commercial gateway – and anchoring North Korea inside China’s economic orbit achieves Beijing’s goals without the diplomatic costs of a three-way military pact.
Finally, the bridge’s opening carries a stark message for Washington and Seoul. With US President Donald Trump having already acknowledged North Korea’s “57” nuclear weapons as a practical reality while hinting at a return to leader-level diplomacy, the traditional bargain of trading sanctions relief for denuclearisation is obsolete.
Physical infrastructure is destiny. A nuclear-armed North Korea connected by a four-lane highway to China’s industrial heartland and a new road link to Russia is insulated against economic coercion as never before.
If Washington returns to the negotiating table with Pyongyang, it will find that the economic leverage it once hoped to trade away has already been paved over across the Yalu.
Seong-Hyon Lee, PhD, is a senior fellow at the George HW Bush Foundation for US-China Relations and an associate-in-research at the Harvard University Asia Centre. This commentary first appeared on Lowy Institute’s blog, The Interpreter.

The South Korean stock market experienced one of its most violent reversals in recent memory last week. The KOSPI, the country's benchmark index, plummeted almost 8% in a single session last Thursday (as cited in a Reuters report), extending a brutal slide that has erased trillions of won in market value.
This sheer slump has put a spotlight squarely on South Korean stocks and, by extension, the exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that hold them.
Amid this backdrop, investors holding South Korean ETFs might be questioning whether this is a sign to exit the market or if this provides an entry point opportunity that needs to be seized.
To answer that question, investors must look closely at what led to the slump and whether it will last long or is just a temporary blip so that they can make an informed decision.
What Led to the Recent Slump?
The rout was not a broad-based economic failure but a highly concentrated shock emanating from the semiconductor sector.
The trigger was primarily a global AI selloff fueled by hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data, which revived fears that interest rates would stay higher for longer. As a result, investors began questioning whether the massive capital expenditure on artificial intelligence would generate sustainable returns amid high rates and started to pull back from semiconductor stocks.
This caused memory chip giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, accounting for nearly half of the KOSPI's total market capitalization, to slump substantially last week. Both these stocks have also been tanking early last week over concerns about intensifying competition from China. Together, these factors led SK Hynix to tank more than 20% last week, while Samsung shares plunged nearly 18%, which ultimately culminated in the whole South Korean stock market suffering a severe market collapse.
In particular, foreign investors have been the primary sellers, offloading a net 176 trillion won worth of Samsung and SK Hynix shares this year, which represented 86% of total foreign net selling in the KOSPI main board, per data released by the Korea Exchange, as of Oct. 14., 2026.
Will This Last Long? The Long-Term Outlook
Despite the panic, South Korea's long-term fundamentals remain remarkably robust, suggesting this may be a painful but temporary correction rather than a structural breakdown.
The International Monetary Fund (“IMF”) recently raised its 2026 growth forecast for South Korea to 3.3%, a significant 0.7 percentage point upgrade from its July projection, citing strong semiconductor exports that are more than offsetting geopolitical headwinds. The IMF also estimates that South Korea's potential growth rate will rise for two consecutive years—to 2.14% this year and 2.20% next year—marking the first back-to-back increase in four decades (per data from the IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook).
Valuations have also compressed to levels that historically signal a bottom. At the 5,000-point level for the KOSPI, the 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio falls to just 4.1 times, with a price-to-book ratio of 1.1 times—lower than the troughs seen during previous volatility episodes in March and July of this year (per a recent report from Samsung Securities).
To this end, Samsung Securities notes that unless earnings forecasts deteriorate materially, the 5,000-point line should serve as support to boost performance of KOSPI in the days ahead.
Looking ahead, clear catalysts for a recovery in the South Korean stock market are on the horizon. Both Samsung and SK Hynix are scheduled to report third-quarter results later this month, which should provide clarity on chip demand and supply outlooks. Furthermore, the U.S. midterm elections in early November should reduce macro-political uncertainty, while the anticipated IPO of AI company Anthropic in mid-November could help stabilize broader AI market sentiment once the initial event volatility subsides.
Buying the Dip: The Case for South Korean ETFs
Considering this growth outlook for the South Korean stock market, one might reasonably conclude that buying the dip in South Korean equities now is a strategy to gain more in the future.
The combination of upgraded IMF growth forecasts, historically low valuations and identifiable near-term catalysts suggests that the current panic-driven selloff may be offering long-term investors a rare entry point into one of Asia's most dynamic economies.

articles.summary: Following Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, semiconductor small managers (materials, parts, and equi..  매일경제
articles.full_text:
The fund has achieved a return of 84.86% in just one year after the establishment of the fund
Plans to expand to a sub-director of a large semiconductor order
The management of volatility through finance and energy is also carried out at the same time
Following Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, semiconductor small managers (materials, parts, and equipment) are expected to emerge as the next players to lead the stock market. Despite the recent plunge in the stock market, the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry will continue, and experts suggest that it is time to expand the investment target from large memory stocks to small managers, drawing attention from investors.
On the 19th, NH Amundi Asset Management announced its management strategy plan at a press conference marking the first anniversary of the launch of the "growth-led Korea Fund" at FKI Tower in Yeouido, Seoul.
The growth-led Korea Fund, which was set up on October 14 last year, is an active stock fund that invests in domestic companies that lead "AI Great Transformation" (AX), "Capital Market Great Transformation" (CX) and "Eco-friendly Great Transformation" (GX). As of the 14th, the first anniversary of the establishment, net assets recorded 130.1 billion won.
Since the establishment, the one-year yield has been 84.86% before the remuneration deduction, exceeding the KOSPI's growth rate of 67.63% by 17.23 percentage points during the same period. Since the beginning of the year, the yield has been 55.02%, 12.44 percentage points higher than the KOSPI. However, the yield for the last three months was -12.64%, slightly below the KOSPI (-12.37%).
Choi Chi-hyun, deputy head of NH Amundi Asset Management's stock management division 2, who manages the fund, cited semiconductors and IT hardware as the key factors that led to its performance. It is explained that the strategy of increasing the proportion of investment in industries and stocks that are expected to benefit from the growth of the AI industry was effective. The financial, platform, and software industries also accumulated excess profits through stock selection. In the future, it plans to expand its investment strategy centered on large semiconductor stocks to small and medium-sized small-sized companies.
"In order to generate additional excess profits, a strategy centered on small and medium-sized stocks that can show higher growth rates next year may be effective," Choi said.
In particular, Choi stressed that core strategies centered on semiconductors and IT hardware are valid even in high-interest-rate environments, but changes are needed in the focus of large-cap stocks centered on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Unlike last year, when Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix's profit forecasts were raised steeply, the pace of increase has slowed recently.
He focused his future operations on expanding investment targets in the AI industry. While maintaining large memory semiconductor stocks as major investment targets, the strategy is to secure additional profits by transferring some of the weight to small manager companies.
"Memory semiconductor companies have a slower profit growth next year compared to this year, but equipment companies can expect a higher growth rate next year than this year as full-fledged investments such as the operation of new factories and expansion of production capacity are underway," Choi said.
"The possibility of outsourcing general-purpose memories to post-processes in the process of expanding Samsung Electronics' production of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is also a factor that changes the small manager industry," he said.
In IT hardware, packaging substrates were presented as a promising field. Analysts say that as semiconductor performance improves, the area of the substrate increases and the number of layers to be stacked increases, it may be difficult to meet demand only with existing production capabilities.
In order to reduce the risk of high interest rates, banks and insurance stocks will be used to respond. In particular, insurance can expect to improve insurance profits and losses and expand shareholder returns due to the reorganization of regulations related to cancellation refund reserves. Crude oil and natural gas-related industries were also proposed as investment targets in preparation for rising raw material prices.
Industries other than AI paid attention to the possibility of recovering the performance of secondary batteries. It is said that shipments can be expected to increase next year, focusing on expanding demand for energy storage (ESS). On the other hand, industrial goods should be cautious in investing just because their stock prices have fallen at a time when no expansion of orders has been confirmed.
Park Jin-ho, head of NH Amundi Asset Management's stock management division, said, "It is the result of the burden of financing by customers, intensifying competition, and realizing profits from soaring stock prices."
However, he found it difficult to interpret this as a weakening of the overall growth engine of the AI industry. This is because the spread of AI agents can increase the demand for memory needed to store users' information and maintain the context of their work.
"Even if OpenAI or Antropic do not do well in the initial public offering (IPO), it is not the end of AI," said Park, head of the division. "A new business model can lead to a new strong person."
He pointed out that it is necessary to confirm the continuity of semiconductor profits in order to re-evaluate Korean stocks. If confidence builds that long-term supply contracts actually lead to stable performance, market concerns about economic volatility in the memory industry can also be alleviated.
"Expanding shareholder returns, such as dividends and treasury stock purchases, is also a factor that will support the stock market," said Park, head of the division. "Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix's combined shareholder returns could reach about 300 trillion won next year."
Citing Apple's example of large-scale shareholder returns even after profit growth slowed, he explained that the implementation and continuity of the reduction policy are also important for domestic semiconductor companies.
"Although Samsung Electronics is an economy-sensitive company, we believe it can be reevaluated if it keeps its promise to return shareholders," said Park, head of the division. "Shareholder return will supply liquidity to the market and support the market."
The government's investment in eco-friendly industries was also cited as an opportunity to discover new growth companies. If investment funds flow into batteries, electric vehicles, and small module reactors (SMR), growth engines may appear in other fields besides AI semiconductors.
Finally, he argued that active funds could also play a role in easing market volatility.
"The active fund must grow to serve as a buffer for the market," said Park, head of the division. "We need tax incentives for fund investment so that it can play a role in selling when stock prices rise and buying when they go down."
